contradictions.question: Is it a a good thing to be childish?
contradictions.summary: The Synoptic Jesus tells his followers they must become like little children to enter the kingdom — receive it, in fact, *as* a little child or stay locked out. Paul tells the Corinthians and the Ephesians the exact opposite: grow up, put away childish things, stop being kids tossed around by every wind of doctrine. Same word-family, same target audience, two different verdicts on whether being childlike is a virtue or a defect.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist playbook here is to draw a distinction between *childlike* and *childish* — Jesus is supposedly praising trust and humility, Paul is supposedly attacking immaturity. Davies and Allison make a version of this move in their ICC Matthew commentary, noting that the Matthean child-saying is about status reversal and dependence rather than cognitive immaturity. Fair enough as a reading of Matt 18:3 in isolation. The trouble is that Paul in 1 Cor 13:11 uses *nēpios* — a Greek word also applied to Jesus' favored hearers in Matt 11:25 ('revealed unto babes,' *nēpioi*) — as a developmental stage to be left behind. The Synoptic kingdom-saying itself uses *paidion/paidia* rather than *nēpios* (Mark 10:15, Matt 18:3), but the broader child-imagery cluster overlaps lexically and conceptually. Hans Conzelmann in the Hermeneia 1 Corinthians treats *nēpios* in 13:11 as straightforwardly negative — childhood is the figure of incomplete knowledge, contrasted with adult *teleios* perfection. Paul then doubles down in 1 Cor 14:20: be infants in malice, but in *understanding* be adults. Ephesians 4:14 pushes the same line. So the harmonization only works if you cherry-pick which features of childhood count: humility yes, ignorance no. The texts themselves don't make that distinction cleanly. Jesus in Matt 11:25 actually thanks the Father for hiding things from the wise and revealing them to *nēpioi* — exactly the cognitive infancy Paul wants his churches to outgrow. That is of course a tension internal to early Christian paraenesis, not a knock-down logical contradiction, but the harmonization requires a finer-grained anthropology than either author supplies.

contradictions.question: What was Jesus' sixth commandment?
contradictions.summary: In the rich young ruler pericope, Jesus enumerates a list of commandments from the Decalogue. Matthew's list has six items ending with 'love thy neighbor as thyself' as number six. Mark's list also has six items but ends with 'honour thy father and mother' as number six and adds a non-Decalogue 'defraud not.' Luke's list has only five items and drops the parental commandment entirely from the sixth position. Three evangelists, three different versions of which commandment Jesus put sixth.
contradictions.commentary: The standard harmonization is that Jesus rattled off the commandments in slightly different orders on different occasions, or that each evangelist is offering a partial summary, not a transcript. The apologist version of this move shows up in Archer and in Blomberg's NAC Matthew. The problem is that the Synoptics are pretty clearly working from a common source here — Markan priority is the consensus position, and Matthew and Luke are demonstrably editing Mark. So the divergence isn't three independent eyewitness reports trailing off in different directions. It's two later editors reshaping the source. Mark's order (adultery, kill, steal, false witness, defraud not, honour parents) actually inverts the LXX/MT order on murder and adultery and inserts 'defraud not,' which isn't in the Decalogue at all — Joel Marcus in the AYB Mark notes the 'defraud not' is likely a gloss reflecting either the tenth commandment on coveting or Sirach 4:1. Matthew (NAC) cleans Mark up: restores the canonical order, drops 'defraud not,' and adds the second great commandment 'love thy neighbor' as a climax — because Matthew wants the encounter to telescope into the Great Commandment debate later in his gospel. Luke shortens the list and reorders. Each evangelist is shaping the tradition to fit his theological program. That's not a transcript problem, that's redaction. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, you can argue Jesus said different things on different occasions. But the three accounts are clearly the *same* pericope — same young man, same wealth question, same answer about selling possessions — so 'different occasions' doesn't survive contact with the parallel structure. Take your pick: redaction or three separate near-identical interviews.

contradictions.question: Is Jesus good?
contradictions.summary: John's Jesus calls himself the good shepherd twice in chapter 10 and applies the adjective *kalos* directly to himself. The Synoptic Jesus, addressed as 'Good Master' by the rich young ruler, deflects the title: 'Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is, God.' One Jesus claims goodness as a self-identifying title; the other refuses it as something only God can hold.
contradictions.commentary: The harmonization most apologists reach for here is that the Synoptic Jesus isn't denying his own goodness, he's testing the rich young ruler — *if* you call me good, you should recognize what that implies about my divine identity. Carson's commentary on Matthew runs this line, as does Blomberg's NAC. It's a clever reading but it has to do a lot of work. The simpler reading is what Markan priority delivers: Mark 10:18 has Jesus straightforwardly rejecting the title, and Matthew edits the saying to soften the divinity problem by changing 'why callest thou me good' to 'why askest thou me concerning the good' (Matt 19:17 in the better manuscripts — the KJV reading reflects later scribal harmonization to Mark/Luke). That edit is exactly what you'd expect if Matthew, writing later and with a higher Christology, was uncomfortable with Mark's wording. Joel Marcus in AYB Mark and Bart Ehrman in *The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture* both treat this as a textbook case of redactional Christology: Mark preserves a saying where Jesus distinguishes himself from God, Matthew rewrites it to remove the distinction, John (which is later still and has the highest Christology of the four) has Jesus openly calling himself *kalos* and claiming functional identity with the Father. John 10:11 and 10:30 together — 'I am the good shepherd' and 'I and the Father are one' — would have been theologically unsayable in Mark's framework. The apologetic reading requires you to read Mark through John. Critical scholarship reads them as developmental stages. *Note: bibleReferences[] contains the malformed entry '14' without book prefix — should read 'John 10:14'. Flag for DB maintainers.*

contradictions.question: Who asked Jesus for the best seats in heaven?
contradictions.summary: In Mark 10:35-37, James and John themselves come to Jesus and ask for the seats at his right and left in his glory. In Matthew 20:20-21, the mother of Zebedee's sons does the asking on their behalf. Same Markan pericope, same request, same place in the narrative — but the petitioner has changed from the disciples to their mother.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleanest examples of Matthean redaction softening an embarrassing tradition in Mark. Mark's James and John look greedy and obtuse — they've just heard Jesus predict his passion for the third time, and their response is to angle for the best seats. Matthew, writing later and trying to protect the reputations of the apostles who will become the pillars of the church, shifts the request to their mother. The disciples are still present and still implicated (Jesus answers *them*, in the plural, in Matt 20:22), but the actual ask comes from a third party. Davies and Allison in the ICC Matthew straightforwardly treat this as redactional embarrassment-management — Matthew is consistently more protective of the Twelve than Mark is. Joel Marcus in AYB Mark concurs. The apologist response — that both happened, the mother spoke first and then the sons spoke for themselves, or vice versa — has to invent a narrative neither evangelist tells. Matt 20:22 has Jesus replying directly to the sons ('ye know not what ye ask'), which only makes sense if they were doing the asking, but Matthew has *just* told us their mother did. The textual seam shows. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, family delegations were a thing in honor-shame culture, and a mother lobbying for her sons is plausible Mediterranean social behavior — Bruce Malina's work on this is solid. But that doesn't explain why Mark, the earlier source, doesn't mention her. The simpler explanation is editorial: Matthew added the mother to shield the apostles. That is of course an inference from redaction, but it's the parsimonious one.

contradictions.question: How much power did Jesus have?
contradictions.summary: Matt 20:23 has Jesus admit that assigning the right- and left-hand seats in his kingdom 'is not mine to give' — that prerogative belongs to the Father. Mark 6:5 reports that in his hometown 'he could there do no mighty work' because of the people's unbelief. Then Matt 28:18, post-resurrection, has Jesus claiming 'all power is given unto me in heaven and in earth,' echoed by John 3:35. So either Jesus had real limits on his power and authority, or he had universal omnipotence — the texts assert both.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologetic harmonization is kenotic: during the incarnation Jesus voluntarily set aside or did not exercise his full divine prerogatives, and only post-resurrection did he reclaim them. This is the classical reading developed from Phil 2:6-8 and systematized by Charles Hodge and modern evangelicals like Grudem. It does some real work. The trouble is Mark 6:5's *ouk edynato* — he was *not able*. Mark doesn't say Jesus *chose not to*, he says he *could not*. Matthew, reading Mark, found that wording theologically intolerable and edited it to 'he did not many mighty works there' (Matt 13:58) — exactly the kind of redactional softening you'd expect. Joel Marcus and R. T. France both note this is one of the clearest cases of Matthean dogmatic correction. The 'not mine to give' saying in Matt 20:23 is harder still: kenotic theory predicts limitations on Jesus' *human nature*, but the right- and left-hand seats in the eschatological kingdom are heavenly assignments — not something the human Jesus would be deciding from Galilee. Why would the Son need to defer to the Father about that *if* he and the Father are functionally one, as John 10:30 claims? The Synoptic Christology and the Matt 28:18 universal-authority Christology are doing different theological work. Bart Ehrman's *How Jesus Became God* lays out the developmental trajectory — Jesus' authority is exalted incrementally across the canonical sources. Steel-manning kenosis: yes, you can square these by stipulating that Christ's omnipotence was masked during incarnation and revealed at exaltation. But the simpler explanation is that Mark, Matthew, and John have different Christologies, and the canon preserves all three without harmonizing them.

contradictions.question: Was Jesus a ransom for many or for all?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 20:28 and Mark 10:45 have Jesus give his life as a *lytron anti pollōn* — a ransom for many. 1 Timothy 2:6 says he gave himself a *antilytron hyper pantōn* — a ransom for all. One says many, the other says all. Whether the atonement is universal or limited rides on which Greek word you read.
contradictions.commentary: This is the textual fault line that runs through the entire Reformed-Arminian debate on the extent of the atonement. Calvinist readers like John Owen in *The Death of Death in the Death of Christ* lean hard on Mark 10:45's *pollōn* (many) and argue the Pastoral 'all' really means 'all kinds of people' or 'all the elect.' Arminian and Wesleyan readers do the reverse, reading the Synoptic 'many' as a Semitism that includes everyone. The harmonization most modern commentators reach for is the Semitism argument: Joachim Jeremias in *The Eucharistic Words of Jesus* famously argued that *rabbim* in Aramaic and Hebrew functions inclusively rather than exclusively — 'the many' as 'the great multitude,' i.e. everyone. Isaiah 53:11-12, the Suffering Servant background Mark 10:45 is clearly echoing, uses *rabbim* in that inclusive sense. That's the steel-man case for harmony. The trouble is that even granting Jeremias the Semitism move, the Greek word *pollōn* in Mark and Matthew is the standard exclusive-of-some word in Greek — and the Pastor of 1 Timothy felt the need to change it to *pantōn*. That change is itself evidence the early church saw a problem with *pollōn* and corrected toward universalism. Whether 1 Timothy was written by Paul (mainstream critical view: deutero-Pauline, late first century — see Raymond Brown's *Introduction to the New Testament*) or by Paul himself, the rewording is editorial. So the contradiction is real at the level of the Greek text even if the underlying theology can be massaged toward harmony. Take your pick: the synoptic Jesus says many, the Pastor says all, and the difference matters enough that fifteen centuries of soteriology have been fought over it.

contradictions.question: How many blind men were healed near Jericho?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 20:30 has Jesus healing two blind men as he leaves Jericho. Mark 10:46 has him healing one named blind man — Bartimaeus son of Timaeus — also leaving Jericho. Luke 18:35 has him healing one unnamed blind man, but *as he was coming nigh unto* Jericho, not leaving. Three Synoptic accounts, three different counts and directions.
contradictions.commentary: The classical apologist harmonization, going back to Augustine's *De Consensu Evangelistarum*, is that there were actually two healings — one as Jesus approached Jericho (Luke's account, of an unnamed man) and one as he left (Mark and Matthew's Bartimaeus story) — and that Matthew just consolidated a second man from another encounter. Or alternatively, that Bartimaeus had a companion who Mark and Luke didn't bother to name. Archer runs this version, as does Blomberg's *The Historical Reliability of the Gospels*. The problem is that it requires inventing healings the texts don't describe and treating the parallel narrative structure as coincidence. Joel Marcus in AYB Mark and Joseph Fitzmyer in AB Luke both treat these as the *same* underlying tradition redacted differently — Markan priority, Matthew and Luke editing Mark independently. Matthew doubles characters elsewhere too (the Gadarene demoniacs in Matt 8:28 vs the one demoniac in Mark 5:2, two donkeys in Matt 21:7 vs one in Mark 11:7), which suggests an editorial habit rather than three separate eyewitness incidents. Luke's reversal of direction is harder to explain redactionally — Fitzmyer suggests Luke moved the healing to the approach so he could give Jericho narrative space for the Zacchaeus story (Luke 19) before the triumphal entry. The Augustinian 'two separate healings' move multiplies miracles to save inerrancy. Steel-man: yes, traveling preachers heal blind men more than once. But the verbal overlap between the three accounts is too tight for that to be the most parsimonious read. Take your pick: redactional variation on one event or three near-identical events that just happen to all cluster around Jericho with the same dialogue.

contradictions.question: When did Jesus' temple tantrum occur?
contradictions.summary: John 2 places Jesus' violent cleansing of the temple at the very beginning of his public ministry, right after the Cana wedding miracle and years before his arrest. The Synoptics place it at the very end of his ministry: Luke 19 has him doing it the same day as the triumphal entry, Matthew 21 and Mark 11 have him doing it the day after. So depending on which gospel you read, the temple action either kicked off Jesus' career or sealed his death warrant in the final week.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the most chewed-over chronological problems in the four-gospel canon, and the apologist solution is to multiply incidents — D. A. Carson, Leon Morris, and Andreas Köstenberger all argue Jesus cleansed the temple *twice*, once at the start of his ministry (John) and once at the end (Synoptics). It's a clean harmonization on paper. The trouble is that the temple action in the Synoptics is precisely what triggers the arrest and execution sequence — Mark 11:18, 'and the scribes and chief priests heard it, and sought how they might destroy him.' If Jesus had already done this same violent demonstration two or three years earlier without consequence, the trigger function in the Synoptic narrative becomes incoherent. Raymond Brown in his AB John lays this out: a public assault on the temple economy was the kind of act the authorities couldn't ignore once, let alone twice. E. P. Sanders' *Jesus and Judaism* makes the temple action the historical lynchpin of Jesus' arrest — the symbolic destruction of the temple is what got him killed within the week. The critical consensus is that John has moved the temple cleansing forward in his narrative for theological reasons — John 2:19's 'destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up' lets the evangelist front-load the resurrection symbolism and frame Jesus' entire ministry as the replacement of temple worship (cf. John 4:21-24). Sandra Schneiders and Marianne Meye Thompson both treat the relocation as Johannine redaction, not historical doublet. Steel-manning the two-cleansings view: John's account has details (the scourge of cords, the whip-driving of the animals) that the Synoptics lack, suggesting independent tradition. Fair. But that proves John had his own source, not that the event happened twice. Take your pick: one event placed in different narrative positions by evangelists with different theological agendas, or two near-identical violent demonstrations that somehow only produced the death penalty the second time.

contradictions.question: On the day that Jesus rode into Jerusalem, did Jesus ask his disciples to get one animal or two?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 21:1-7 has Jesus dispatch two disciples to fetch *an ass and her colt*, and the disciples bring back both animals; Matthew even depicts Jesus sitting on the garments laid across both. Mark 11:1-7 and Luke 19:28-35 mention only a single colt. John 12:14 has Jesus find a young ass himself, without dispatching anyone. One Triumphal Entry, four different vehicles.
contradictions.commentary: Matthew's two-animal version is a textbook case of an evangelist over-literalizing a Hebrew prophecy. The Zechariah 9:9 oracle Matthew is explicitly citing — 'thy King cometh unto thee, lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass' — uses standard Hebrew synonymous parallelism, where the same animal is named twice in different terms. Zechariah is talking about one donkey, described two ways. Matthew, reading the Greek of the LXX where the parallelism is preserved as 'an ass and a colt,' apparently took it as two separate animals and adjusted his narrative accordingly. Davies and Allison in the ICC are explicit: 'Matthew has misunderstood the Hebrew parallelism.' Joel Marcus calls it 'over-literal exegesis.' R. T. France, who is generally sympathetic to Matthew's reliability, concedes the parallelism point and tries to rescue the situation by suggesting the mother donkey was brought along to keep the unbroken colt calm — a plausible animal-handling note but one Matthew never makes. The apologist harmonization typically runs along France's lines or argues that Mark and Luke 'simplified' to one animal. The problem with the simplification argument is that Mark and Luke are *earlier* than Matthew in the consensus chronology, so they aren't simplifying Matthew — Matthew is *complicating* them. The simpler reading is that the Synoptic tradition knew one animal, Zechariah's parallelism got read literally somewhere in Matthean redaction, and a second donkey appeared in the narrative to fit the prophecy. That is of course an inference from redaction-critical method, but the alternative is to posit that Jesus deliberately rode two animals simultaneously to fulfill a misreading of Zechariah. John, meanwhile, sidesteps the whole disciple-dispatch tradition by having Jesus find the donkey himself — a separate redactional path. Take your pick: Matthew misread the Hebrew, or Jesus straddled two donkeys.

contradictions.question: When did Jesus curse the fig tree?
contradictions.summary: Mark 11:12-17 has Jesus curse the barren fig tree on the way *into* Jerusalem, *then* enter the temple and cleanse it. Matthew 21:12-19 reverses the sequence: Jesus first cleanses the temple, then leaves to Bethany, and only the next morning curses the fig tree. Same two events, opposite order.
contradictions.commentary: Mark deliberately interweaves the cursing and the cleansing as a single sandwich (Markan intercalation): the temple is the fig tree, judged for its lack of fruit. Joel Marcus and R. T. France both treat this as one of the cleanest examples of Markan literary technique — the fig tree frames the temple cleansing as an enacted parable of judgment. Mark even goes out of his way to tell us *it was not the season for figs* (11:13), which sounds like a contradiction until you read it as part of the symbolic frame: the temple is also out of season, also fruitless, also under judgment. Matthew, working from Mark, doesn't preserve the intercalation. He compresses the two-day Markan sequence into a single-event narrative where the fig tree withers immediately after the cursing and the temple cleansing has been moved up to the previous day. Davies and Allison call this Matthean simplification — the evangelist trades Mark's literary structure for a tighter narrative. The apologist harmonization, found in Carson and Blomberg, is that Matthew is summarizing thematically while Mark is reporting chronologically, so the contradiction is only apparent. That works as a *historiographical* description of what Matthew is doing, but it concedes the point: the events did not happen in the same chronological order in both accounts, and only one of the two evangelists can be giving the actual sequence. The critical scholarship treats Mark as preserving the literary intercalation and Matthew as having dismantled it for narrative economy. Steel-man: ancient historians did rearrange events for thematic purposes and that was a respected technique. Fair enough. But conceding that means conceding that the gospels are not chronological transcripts — which is exactly the point. Take your pick: Mark has the right order or Matthew does, but they can't both be reporting the historical sequence.

contradictions.question: When did the cursed fig tree die?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 21:19-20 says the fig tree 'presently' withered after Jesus cursed it, and the disciples marveled at the speed: 'How soon is the fig tree withered away!' Mark 11:13-14, 20-21 has the disciples observe the cursed tree only the *next morning*, withered from the roots — and Peter has to remind Jesus what he said the day before. Matthew's tree dies instantly; Mark's takes overnight.
contradictions.commentary: This pairs directly with the previous contradiction (id 450) on the *order* of the cursing and the temple cleansing. Once Matthew collapses Mark's two-day intercalated sequence into a single-event narrative, the timing of the tree's death gets compressed too. In Mark the natural reading is: day one, Jesus curses the tree on the way into Jerusalem; day two, walking back from Bethany, the disciples notice it has withered overnight. In Matthew, since the cursing and the discovery are part of the same scene, the tree has to die immediately — *parachrēma*, 'at once.' Davies and Allison flag this as one of Matthew's most obvious editorial intensifications of Mark's miracle traditions. Matthew does this elsewhere: in Matt 8:13 the centurion's servant is healed *in that hour* (Luke 7:10 just has him healed when the messengers return); in Matt 9:22 the hemorrhaging woman is healed *from that hour* (Mark 5:29 has her flow dry *immediately* but Matthew adds the formal time marker). The pattern is Matthean redactional intensification: miracles get faster and more dramatic. The apologist harmonization is that Matthew is telescoping — the withering happened overnight as Mark says, but Matthew compresses the timeline for narrative impact. Archer and Blomberg both run a version of this. The harmonization concedes the editorial point: the gospels do not record events in the same time-scale, and one or both authors are shaping the chronology for effect. Bart Ehrman in *Jesus, Interrupted* uses this exact pericope as a case study: the contradiction isn't a manuscript glitch, it's the result of two authors with different storytelling priorities. Steel-manning the telescoping defense: yes, ancient writers compressed events all the time. But that means at least one of these accounts is not a chronological transcript — which is the contradiction the question is asking about.

contradictions.question: Should we do what the Pharisees say to do?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 23:1-3 has Jesus tell the crowds that because the scribes and Pharisees 'sit in Moses' seat,' the listeners should 'observe and do' whatever the Pharisees tell them — just don't imitate their behavior. Matthew 16:12, by contrast, has the disciples finally understand Jesus' warning that they should beware 'the doctrine of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees.' Same gospel, two opposite instructions about whether to follow Pharisaic teaching.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the most internally tangled passages in Matthew, and even friendly commentators concede there's a real tension here. The Matt 23:2-3 saying is unique to Matthew — no parallel in Mark or Luke — and it sits at the head of a chapter that then proceeds to lambast the Pharisees in the harshest terms anywhere in the gospels ('woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites,' seven times). Davies and Allison in the ICC wrestle with this for several pages and conclude that 23:2-3 is best understood as a piece of inherited Matthean tradition the evangelist did not fully integrate, possibly reflecting an earlier stratum where Jesus' Jewish-Christian followers still operated within Pharisaic authority structures. Anthony Saldarini's *Matthew's Christian-Jewish Community* runs this line in detail: the saying reflects a community still legally Jewish, still under Pharisaic juridical authority, even as it is in bitter polemical conflict with Pharisaic leadership. So historically the contradiction reflects two layers of Matthean community life. The apologist harmonization is that Jesus was telling his audience to obey the Pharisees *only when* the Pharisees taught Mosaic law correctly — the 'sit in Moses' seat' qualifier limits the command to legitimate Torah interpretation, and Matt 16:12's warning about 'doctrine' refers to the Pharisees' *additional* teaching, their 'tradition of the elders.' That works as a logical reconciliation but it requires inserting a qualifier ('only when they teach Moses faithfully') that the text itself doesn't supply. Mark Allan Powell's argument that 23:3's 'observe and do' really means 'observe what they observe' — that is, watch their practice — is grammatically possible but most translators reject it. Ulrich Luz in Hermeneia treats the verse as an unresolved fossil. Steel-man: Matthew may be distinguishing positional authority (the seat) from personal authority (the men), and telling readers to respect the office while ignoring the officeholders. That distinction works for institutional theology but not as a coherent halakhic instruction.

contradictions.question: When will the end of the world come?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 10:23 has Jesus tell the Twelve they will not finish evangelizing the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes. Matthew 24:14 has the same Jesus declare that the gospel must first be preached *in all the world for a witness unto all nations, and then shall the end come*. One verse limits the eschaton to a window inside the disciples' Israelite mission; the other requires worldwide proclamation as a precondition.
contradictions.commentary: Matthew 10:23 is one of the most embarrassing verses in the New Testament for traditional eschatology, and Albert Schweitzer made it the lynchpin of his *Quest of the Historical Jesus* — Jesus expected the Parousia imminently, within the lifetime of the men he was sending out on this very mission, and he was simply wrong. Schweitzer's reading remains the consensus in critical scholarship: Dale Allison's *Jesus of Nazareth: Millenarian Prophet* and E. P. Sanders' *The Historical Figure of Jesus* both treat 10:23 as authentic dominical eschatology with a clear and falsified time horizon. Matt 24:14, on the other hand, sits in the apocalyptic discourse and reflects a later horizon — the gospel has to reach 'all nations,' a missionary program that only makes sense after the Easter experience and the Gentile mission opened up by Paul and others. Davies and Allison in the ICC suggest 10:23 and 24:14 reflect different traditions Matthew has stitched together: the older Jewish-mission saying (10:23) and the post-resurrection universal-mission saying (24:14). The apologist harmonization typically runs along two lines. The first, going back to Calvin and recently defended by Carson, is that 'the Son of Man's coming' in 10:23 refers not to the Parousia but to the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE — Jesus 'came in judgment' on the temple. That works as a typological reading but it requires importing a non-obvious referent into the saying. The second is the partial-preterist move: 10:23 has been *partially* fulfilled and is still in progress. France runs a version of this. The trouble is that 10:23 specifies the disciples will *not have finished* before the coming — that's not a partial fulfillment, it's a deadline. Bart Ehrman in *Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium* lays out the case that Jesus was a thoroughgoing apocalypticist whose timetable was simply incorrect, and Matt 10:23 is exhibit A. Take your pick: Jesus expected the imminent end and was wrong, or 'the Son of Man's coming' shifts referent between 10:23 and 24:14 in ways the text never signals.

contradictions.question: When did Jesus say he would return?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 10:23 promises the Son of Man's return before the Twelve finish their preaching tour of Israel. Matthew 24:14 promises that the end will come only after the gospel has been preached to all nations of the earth. The same gospel offers two incompatible timetables for the same eschatological event.
contradictions.commentary: This is essentially the same problem as id 453, asked from the Parousia angle rather than the end-of-the-age angle. The apparent contradiction sharpens when you stack the explicit time-window sayings together: Matt 10:23 ('ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come'), Matt 16:28 ('there be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom'), Matt 24:34 ('this generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled'), and Mark 9:1 / Mark 13:30 in parallel. Every one of these saying-types limits the return to within the first generation of Jesus' followers. Matt 24:14, by contrast, opens up the timeline to allow for worldwide proclamation. Critical scholarship reads this as the tension between the historical Jesus' authentic apocalyptic preaching — which assumed imminent intervention — and the early church's *Naherwartung* crisis after the first generation died without the Parousia arriving (2 Pet 3:4 explicitly addresses the embarrassment: 'Where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were'). Dale Allison and E. P. Sanders both treat the time-window sayings as among the most historically secure dominical material precisely because they are *embarrassing* — the church would not have invented predictions that failed. C. H. Dodd's 'realized eschatology' tried to dissolve the problem by reading the kingdom sayings non-temporally, but most critical scholars after Allison have returned to consistent eschatology. The apologist harmonization tracks what was said for the previous contradiction: 'coming of the Son of Man' in 10:23 is reinterpreted as either the 70 CE temple destruction (Carson, France) or the post-Easter inauguration of the new age (N. T. Wright in *Jesus and the Victory of God*). Wright's reading is the most sophisticated apologetic move on the table and worth steel-manning: the 'coming' is metaphorical-political, Jesus' vindication and the destruction of the old temple-economy. But Wright's reading still has to handle Matt 16:28's *some standing here* will not taste death — a generational marker that doesn't fit Wright's metaphorical Parousia comfortably. Take your pick: imminent apocalyptic and falsified, or radically re-symbolized in ways the early church never figured out.

contradictions.question: Will Jesus's second coming be visible to all?
contradictions.summary: The Synoptic apocalyptic discourses and Revelation 1:7 stack up to say the return of the Son of Man will be a universally visible event: every tribe of the earth will see him, every eye will see him, he comes on the clouds with great power and glory. John 14:19, by contrast, has Jesus tell the disciples 'yet a little while, and the world seeth me no more.' One stream of texts insists the world will see him; another insists it won't.
contradictions.commentary: The harmonization here is actually pretty defensible if you accept the standard reading of John 14:19 — the verse is set in the upper-room discourse the night before the crucifixion, and 'the world seeth me no more' refers to the period between Jesus' death and his return, not to the Parousia itself. Raymond Brown's AB John commentary reads it this way, and so does Andreas Köstenberger's BECNT John: the disciples will see Jesus post-resurrection and via the Spirit, the unbelieving world will not. On that reading, John 14:19 and the Synoptic Parousia texts aren't talking about the same event — one is about the Easter-to-Parousia interim, the other is about the Parousia itself. So the SAB framing of this contradiction overreaches a bit. That said, there's still a real Christological tension here worth flagging. John's gospel as a whole is significantly less interested in the universally visible Parousia than the Synoptics are. The realized eschatology of John 5:24-25 ('the hour is coming, and now is') and the spiritualized 'coming' of John 14:18 ('I will come to you') push the eschaton inward and present-tense in ways that don't sit easily with Mark 13's apocalyptic spectacle. Rudolf Bultmann famously argued that John has so internalized eschatology that the Synoptic Parousia is essentially redundant in the Fourth Gospel's framework. Subsequent scholars like Charles Dodd and James Dunn have moderated Bultmann's position — there are still future-eschatological elements in John (5:28-29; 6:39-40) — but the gravitational pull of Johannine eschatology is toward present realization, not future visibility. So the contradiction is sharper at the level of overall theological framework than at the level of the specific proof-text the question cites. That is of course a more nuanced read than the question allows. Steel-man for the apologist: John 14:19 is plainly about the post-crucifixion interim and doesn't touch the Parousia. Fair. The deeper tension between Johannine realized eschatology and Synoptic apocalyptic remains a live scholarly issue, but this specific proof-text pairing is on the weaker side. *Note: the contradiction as framed pivots on a verse (John 14:19) that most critical and apologist commentators alike read as referring to the post-crucifixion interim rather than the Parousia. The question may need rewording to target the stronger Johannine-vs-Synoptic eschatological tension (e.g., John 14:18-23 vs Mark 13:26).*

contradictions.question: Did Jesus say before the cock crow or before the cock crows twice?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 26:34, Luke 22:34, and John 13:38 all have Jesus tell Peter he will deny him three times *before the cock crows*. Mark 14:30 alone has Jesus tell Peter the denials will happen *before the cock crows twice*. Three gospels say one crow, the earliest gospel says two.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the small but stubborn synoptic divergences where Mark looks like the more historically specific version and Matthew, Luke, and John have all independently rounded the saying off. On Markan priority — the consensus position — Mark is the source the other Synoptics are working from, so the natural inference is that Matthew and Luke smoothed Mark's distinctive double-crow detail to the simpler single-crow form. Joel Marcus in AYB Mark and R. T. France in NIGTC both treat this as Matthean and Lukan simplification of a more awkward Markan tradition. There's also a textual-criticism wrinkle worth noting: the 'twice' in Mark 14:30 and 14:72 is absent from some manuscripts (Sinaiticus original hand, codex Vaticanus in 14:68 omits the first crow), and Bart Ehrman has argued this may be a case where scribes were trying to harmonize Mark to the other gospels by removing the second crow. The current NA28 critical text retains 'twice' in both verses as the most likely original Markan reading. So Mark probably did say 'twice,' and the other three evangelists or the tradition behind them simplified. The apologist harmonization, found in Archer and Geisler/Howe, is that Jesus said both — Mark preserves the fuller saying, and Matthew, Luke, and John give the abbreviated version. Logically possible but it requires assuming the simpler form is a partial quotation of the fuller form, when the parallel structure suggests instead that the fuller form is the *original* and the simpler is the *redacted*. Steel-man: the differing forms could reflect different tradition streams that knew the saying with or without the doubling, and the evangelists used whichever version reached them. Fair, but on Markan priority the other three are reading Mark — they had the 'twice' in front of them and didn't include it. Take your pick: Markan priority means the others omitted, or some prior tradition was already variable and the evangelists each picked a form.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus ask God to save him from crucifixion?
contradictions.summary: In the Synoptic Gethsemane scene (Matt 26:36-42, Mark 14:35-36, Luke 22:41-42) Jesus prays explicitly that the cup of suffering pass from him — 'let this cup pass from me,' 'take away this cup from me,' 'remove this cup from me.' The Johannine Jesus in John 12:27 raises the same possibility only to dismiss it instantly: 'shall I say, Father, save me from this hour? but for this cause came I unto this hour.' One Jesus actively prays for escape; the other rules the prayer out as a non-starter.
contradictions.commentary: The Gethsemane prayer is one of the most striking divergences between the Synoptic and Johannine portraits of Jesus, and the divergence is fundamental to each gospel's Christology. The Synoptic Jesus is fully human in his anguish — Mark 14:33's *ekthambeisthai kai adēmonein* ('troubled and very heavy') uses the strongest distress vocabulary in the gospel. Luke 22:44 even has him sweating blood (though that verse is text-critically uncertain — NA28 brackets it as a likely later addition). The Johannine Jesus has no Gethsemane scene at all; the whole 'troubled soul' moment is compressed into John 12:27, and even there the prayer for deliverance is voiced only to be rejected. Raymond Brown's *Death of the Messiah* is the definitive treatment: John has deliberately rewritten the agony tradition because Johannine Christology cannot accommodate a Jesus who genuinely wants out. The Fourth Gospel's Jesus is in sovereign control of his own passion ('no man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself,' John 10:18), and that means he cannot be portrayed praying to escape the cross. C. H. Dodd, Rudolf Bultmann, and Ernst Käsemann all read the Johannine omission as theological editing. The apologist harmonization, found in Carson and Köstenberger, is that both moments are real — John 12:27 captures an earlier moment of inner conflict that Jesus resolved before Gethsemane, where he simply repeated for the disciples' benefit the same prayer-and-submission pattern. Plausible enough as a narrative reconstruction, but it requires inferring two separate prayer-incidents the texts don't connect. The harder case for harmony: even granting two events, the *Synoptic* Gethsemane Jesus genuinely entertains the request — 'if it be possible' — while the Johannine Jesus dismisses the request the moment he raises it. Those are not two stages of one psychology; they're two different Christologies. Bart Ehrman in *How Jesus Became God* uses this contrast as a textbook example of the Synoptic-to-John developmental trajectory: as Christology gets higher, Jesus' human frailty gets airbrushed out. Take your pick: two prayer-events with incompatible emotional content, or one event reshaped by Johannine theology.

contradictions.question: Did Judas identify Jesus with a kiss?
contradictions.summary: The three Synoptic arrest scenes (Matt 26:47-49, Mark 14:43-45, Luke 22:47-48) all have Judas identify Jesus by approaching and kissing him — the prearranged signal so the arresting party could pick the right man out of the dark olive grove. John 18:3-5 reports the same arrest but without any kiss; instead Jesus himself steps forward and identifies himself by saying 'I am he,' and the arresting party falls to the ground in awe. Same event, two completely different identification mechanics.
contradictions.commentary: John's omission of the Judas kiss is not just a different detail — it's a deliberate Christological choice. In the Synoptics, Jesus is found, marked, and seized. In John, Jesus is the sovereign actor: he steps forward, asks 'Whom seek ye?', identifies himself with the divine *egō eimi* ('I am'), and the soldiers literally fall down. Raymond Brown in *The Death of the Messiah* argues this is a deliberate Johannine reworking — the Fourth Gospel's Jesus must not be passively identified by a traitor, because that would undercut his sovereign control over the passion. So John omits the kiss and replaces it with a theophanic self-revelation. Bart Ehrman in his textual-criticism work and *How Jesus Became God* makes the same observation: John consistently strips away moments where Jesus appears passive or weak. The apologetic harmonization is that both happened — Judas kissed Jesus (per the Synoptics) and Jesus then stepped forward and announced himself (per John), and each evangelist reports only the part he found relevant. Carson and Köstenberger both run this version. It's not impossible. Honor-shame culture had arrest conventions, and ancient narratives are often selective about which details they preserve. But the *function* of identification is completely different in the two traditions: the Synoptic kiss is necessary because the arresting party couldn't otherwise pick Jesus out (Mark 14:44 has Judas explicitly say 'whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he'); John's self-identification is necessary because Jesus must not be passively identified. Both can't be true *as the actual mechanism of arrest* — either the soldiers needed a sign from Judas or they didn't. The simpler critical reading is that John has rewritten the tradition to remove the passive elements; the Synoptic kiss is more likely historical (it's embarrassing and unlikely to be invented), and the Johannine *egō eimi* is theological. Steel-man for harmony: both events occurred in sequence, with John selecting the dramatic moment. Fair as narrative reconstruction. But the Synoptic insistence that a sign was *needed* and the Johannine insistence that Jesus *volunteered the identification* fight each other on the function of the arrest, not just on which detail to record.

contradictions.question: Was Jesus taken to Caiaphas or Annas first?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 26:57 names Caiaphas explicitly as the high priest Jesus was led to. Mark 14:53 and Luke 22:54 say Jesus was led to 'the high priest,' which in context means Caiaphas, since he was the sitting high priest in 30-36 CE. John 18:13 alone has Jesus taken first to *Annas*, Caiaphas's father-in-law, before being sent to Caiaphas in 18:24. Three gospels go straight to Caiaphas; John inserts an extra hearing before Annas.
contradictions.commentary: The historical situation behind this divergence is genuinely interesting and the harmonization is, on this one, fairly defensible. Annas had been high priest from 6 to 15 CE, then was deposed by the Roman prefect Valerius Gratus, but Josephus (*Antiquities* 20.198) confirms that even after his deposition Annas remained the dominant figure in the high-priestly family — five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas served as high priests over the subsequent decades. The Jewish theological view, attested in the Mishnah, was that the high priest held the office for life regardless of Roman political maneuvering. So Annas was likely still referred to as 'high priest' informally and probably still wielded de facto power. Raymond Brown's *Death of the Messiah* lays this out: the Johannine detail of an Annas hearing isn't implausible at all — Annas may well have been the first stop for any politically sensitive arrest. That's the steel-man case for harmonization, and Köstenberger, Carson, and Bock all run it. The harder problem is that the Synoptics don't *mention* the Annas hearing — they go straight to Caiaphas and the formal Sanhedrin trial. If there was a preliminary hearing at Annas's house, the Synoptics either didn't know about it or didn't think it mattered. John, meanwhile, seems uncertain whether to call Annas or Caiaphas 'the high priest' in 18:19-22 — the Greek is ambiguous, and Brown spends pages on whether the questioning in those verses is happening at Annas's residence or Caiaphas's. Some critical scholars (Bultmann, Käsemann) treat the Annas hearing as a Johannine literary doublet, the evangelist multiplying the trial to deepen the symbolism. Most contemporary commentators (Brown, Marcus, Fitzmyer) consider an Annas hearing historically plausible but flag that John's chronology of the trial is hard to reconcile with the Synoptic Sanhedrin scene. Take your pick: John preserves an extra hearing the Synoptics omitted, or John has expanded the trial sequence for theological emphasis. The contradiction is real at the level of how-many-hearings; the question of who held the title is largely a non-problem once you understand first-century high-priestly politics.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus say, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up"?
contradictions.summary: John 2:19-21 has Jesus straightforwardly speak this saying as a public pronouncement at the temple cleansing, and the narrator helpfully tells us he meant the temple of his body. Matthew 26:59-61 and Mark 14:57-58 report the saying being introduced at Jesus' trial only by *false witnesses* whose testimony was inadmissible because they couldn't even agree on the wording. One gospel has Jesus saying it on the record; two others say it was a slander invented by people trying to get him killed.
contradictions.commentary: This is a fascinating one because it's not a simple denial — Mark and Matthew don't say Jesus *didn't* say something like this, they say the witnesses against him were false and couldn't get the wording straight. So the underlying issue is whether the saying belongs to authentic dominical tradition or to enemy distortion of it. The critical consensus, well-developed in Raymond Brown's *Death of the Messiah*, is that Jesus probably did say *something* about the temple's destruction — the saying meets multiple criteria of authenticity (multiple attestation across Mark, John, Acts 6:14, and likely Gospel of Thomas 71; embarrassment, because it predicts something the temple-loving early church didn't celebrate; coherence with Jesus' Jeremianic temple-action). E. P. Sanders treats the temple-saying as one of the most historically secure items in the Jesus tradition. The Synoptic-Johannine divergence is therefore about *how* the saying was preserved and framed. Mark and Matthew, writing after the temple's actual destruction in 70 CE, find themselves in an awkward position: Jesus' prediction of the temple's fall had become embarrassingly literal, but the *resurrection* application — building it back up in three days — was always going to look like a stretch. So they distance Jesus from the literal wording by attributing it to false witnesses while still letting the saying do its narrative work. John, with a high Christology and an interest in temple-replacement theology, owns the saying outright and helpfully explains it as resurrection symbolism. The apologist harmonization, found in Carson, Köstenberger, and Blomberg, is that both can be true at once: Jesus did say it (per John), but the witnesses at the trial misquoted or distorted what he said (per Mark/Matthew), and that's why their testimony was rejected as 'false.' That actually works — the Synoptic charge is specifically that the witnesses 'agreed not together' (Mark 14:59), not that they invented the saying from nothing. Brown's Death of the Messiah accepts a version of this: a genuine logion got rephrased into a courtroom accusation. Steel-manning the contradiction: even on the harmonizing reading, the Synoptic narrators frame the saying as untrustworthy slander while John frames it as authentic prophecy. The *theological* posture toward the saying is opposed across the gospels even if the underlying historical saying is one. Take your pick: the synoptics protect Jesus from a saying he probably did make, or John explicates a saying his sources had buried.
